# Sallekha Sutta (MN 8 (PTS MN i 40))

**ID:** MN 8 (PTS MN i 40)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Sallekha Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Self-Effacement
**PTS:** MN i 40
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn8
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sallekha Sutta* ("Self-Effacement", MN 8) is the eighth discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, placed in the *Mūlapariyāyavagga* [SuttaCentral; Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi 1995]. The sutta addresses the problem of eradicating dogmatic views concerning the self and the world [Anālayo 2010; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. In response to these views, the Buddha rejects the notion that the attainment of meditative absorptions (*jhāna*s) and formless attainments constitutes true effacement; rather, he designates these attainments as tranquil abidings or "pleasant dwellings here and now" (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*) [Carrithers 2001; Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi 1995; Wen]. Instead, authentic effacement (*sallekha*)—the wearing away of defilements and conceit—is delineated across forty-four ethical and spiritual practices, emphasizing that one who is himself stuck cannot pull another out [SuttaCentral; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. The discourse concludes with a classic exhortation urging the monastics to meditate in remote places and at the roots of trees to avoid future remorse [Didonna & Kabat-Zinn; Polak 2011].

In the Pali commentarial tradition, the sutta's doctrinal density is celebrated: the commentary on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* glosses "profound" (*gambhīra*) as textual difficulty comparable to the *Sallekha Sutta* [Masefield 1994], while the *Papañcasūdanī* explains that meditative absorptions alone do not constitute effacement unless conjoined with insight [Wen]. The text is also cited in the canonical *Cullaniddesa* and *Mahāniddesa* [SuttaCentral]. A full parallel exists in the Sarvāstivāda Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 91, *Zhouna wenjian jing*), with additional parallels in the *Ekottarika-āgama* (EĀ 47.9) [SuttaCentral; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. Machine analysis by DharmaNexus reflects this alignment with Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* passages (T26), alongside thematic matches in the *Dharmaskandha* and *Prajñāpāramitā* corpora [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus records over 1,300 shared passages across 117 texts, sharing substantial formulaic material with the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (AN 9, AN 10, AN 4), the *Mūlapaṇṇāsa-aṭṭhakathā*, and the *Anumāna Sutta* (MN 15) [DharmaNexus].
